【Malliavin 随机分析】1 Wiener Chaos Decomposition

Created2026-11-19|Updated2026-11-19|posts
|Post Views:

DISCLAIMER

This note is based on Malliavin Calculus and Related Topics by David Nualart and is intended solely for personal academic study and should not be regarded as a substitute for the original text.

1 Wiener Chaos Decomposition

We seek a generalized form of Gaussian process, say changing the set of time indices T to a "more abstract" space H . Suppose H is a real separable Hilbert space with innrt product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩H and norm ‖h‖H for h∈H .

Isonormal Gaussian process

Definition 1.1.1. (Gaussian process on H or isonormal Gaussian process)

Stochastic process W={W(h):h∈H} defined on a complete probability space (Ω,F,P) is a Gaussian process on H if W is a centered Gaussian family r.v. and for all h,g∈H , we have E(W(h)W(g))=⟨h,g⟩H

The mapping h↦W(h) can be shown linear (a.s.). As one can expand and compute E[(W(λh+μg)−λW(h)−μW(g))2]=0 using E(W(h)W(g))=⟨h,g⟩H . Since the bilinearity of inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩H , we have E(W(h+k)W(g))=⟨h+k,g⟩H=E((W(h)W(g)))+W(W(k)W(g)) , and E(W(h)W(g+k))=E(W(h)W(g))+E(W(h)W(k)) , thus we have

E[(W(λh+μg)−λW(h)−μW(g))2]=E[W(λh+μg)2]+E[(λW(h)+μW(g))2]−2E[(W(λh+μg))(λW(h)+μW(g))]=0.

This shows that h↦W(h) is an linear isometry from H onto a closed subspace of L2(Ω,F,P) , since linear isometry preserves completeness, L2 space is complete, and thus yields W(H) is closed.

Existance of such probability space. The Kolmogrov extention theorem states that given some probability space (Ω,F,P) , for all k∈N and finite sequence h1,…,hk∈H , then there exists a probability measure on product σ -algebra of ΩH if the measure νh1,…,hk on Ωk satisfies

  1. (Permutation Invariant) Given arbitrary permutation π , k∈N and measurable sets Fhi⊂Ω,i=1,…,k , we have
νh1,…,hk(Fh1,…,Fhk)=νπ(h1),…,π(hk)(Fπ(h1),…,Fπ(hk)),

this means the measure persists when input indices and subscripts are jointly permuted. 2. (Marginal Consistency) Given k,m∈N and measurable sets Fhi⊂Ω,i=1,…,k , we have

νh1,…,hk(Fh1,…,Fhk)=νh1,…,hk,hk+1,…,hk+m(Fh1,…,Fhk,Ω,…,Ω⏟m times),

this tells that the measure is consistent when marginalized out some of its indices.

Then we check whether the isonormal Gaussian process matches the requirements of Kolmogrov extention theorem. Arbitrarily choose h1,…,hk∈H , construct the Gram matrix Σ whose indices Σij=⟨hi,hj⟩H . The Gram matrix Σ is symmetric and positive-semidefinite, which corresponds to a Gaussian distribution N(0,Σ) , and we use this distribution to denote the distribution of (W(h1),…,W(hk)) . We check symmetry conditions first. Given permutation π , there is a corresponding permutation matrix Pπ and the permutated distribution on permutated bases is N(0,PπΣPπ⊤) . To check the equivalence of two Gaussian measures, it suffices to prove the two covariance matrices is identical under the same set of bases. For permuted distribution we have x′⊤PπΣPπ⊤x′=x⊤Pπ⊤PπΣPπ⊤Pπx=x⊤Σx , this shows that the measure is invariant under permutation. For marginal consistency, it suffices to prove that given k,m∈N and h1,…,hk+m , the top left sub-matrix Σk of the big covariance matrix Σk+m corresponds to the very covariance matrix of (W(h1),…,h(hk)) , which is obvious. By Kolmogrov extention theorem, such a measure ν DOES exists.

We use Kolmogrov extention theorem to check the well-definiteness of isonormal Gaussian process. A core block of the definition is the covariance structure.

Relation to Ito Brownian Motion and Ito Stochastic Integral. Recall that for one-dimensinoal Brownian motion W(⋅) , we have E(W(s)W(t))=s∧t , which is symmetric and semidefinite and corresponds to the Cameron-Martin space HCM , which is defined as

HCM={f:[0,T]→R:f(0)=0,f abs. cont.,f′∈L2[0,T]}

and the inner product is ⟨f,g⟩HCM:=∫0Tf′(s)g′(s)ds . Consider the reproducing kernel K(s,t)=s∧t , construct Kt(⋅)=K(⋅,t) , whose weak derivative is 1[0,t] . Introduce the Ito stochastic integral operator W˙:L2[0,T]→L2(R) , Brownian motion B(t) could be expressed as the stochastic integral of identity function 1[0,t] :

W˙(h)=∫0ThdBt,

therefore one could rewrite B(t) as W˙(1[0,t]) . This setting corresponds with the definition of isonormal Gaussian process:

E[W(s)W(t)]=E[W˙(1[0,s])W˙(1[0,t])]=⟨1[0,s],1[0,t]⟩L2=s∧t.

This reveals that W˙ is the isonormal Gaussian process on [0,T] , it also behaves as the isometry, which is the well-known Ito isometry:

E[W˙2(h)]=‖h‖L2.

We seek to decompose L2(Ω,F,P) into orthogonal sum of subspaces, as Taylor expansion allows us to rewrite analytic function into series of functions, we look into Hermite polynomials Hn(x) for similar building blocks in the sense of Ito integration.

Hermite Polynomials

Definition 1.1.2. Hermite Polynomials Hn(x) Hermite Polynomialsn show up when we expand F(x,t)=exp⁡(tx−t22) w.r.t. t :

F(x,t)=exp⁡[x22−12(x−t)2]=exp⁡(x22)∑n=0∞tnn![dndtnexp⁡(−(x−t)22)]t=0=exp⁡(x22)∑n=0∞tn⋅(−1)nn!dndxnexp⁡(−x22)x=x−t=∑n=0∞tn⋅Hn(x).

Lemma 1.1.3. Properties of Hermite Polynomials The Hermite polynomials admit the following properties:

Hn′(x)=Hn−1(x)n⩾1,(n+1)Hn+1(x)=xHn(x)−Hn−1(x),n⩾1,Hn(−x)=(−1)nHn(x),n⩾1.

Proof.

We first prove Hn′(x)=Hn−1(x)

Hn′(x)=ddx{(−1)nn!exp⁡(x22)dndxnexp⁡(−x22)}=(−1)nn!exp⁡(x22)[x⋅dndxnexp⁡(−x22)+dn+1dxn+1exp⁡(−x22)]=(−1)nn!exp⁡(x22)[x⋅dndxnexp⁡(−x22)−xdndxnexp⁡(−x22)−ndn−1dxn−1exp⁡(−x22)]=(−1)n−1(n−1)!dn−1dxn−1exp⁡(−x22)=Hn−1(x).

Note that when proving Hn′(x)=Hn−1(x) , by Leibniz formula, we have

(−1)nn!exp⁡(x22)dn+1dxn+1exp⁡(−x22)=(−1)nn!exp⁡(x22)[−xdndxnexp⁡(−x22)−ndn−1dxn−1exp⁡(−x22)]⟺−(n+1)Hn+1(x)=−xHn(x)+Hn−1(x).

The last statement is straight forward, by performing y=−x , we have ∂y∂x=−1 , therefore ∂∂x=−∂∂y . Applying n times yields ∂n∂xn=(−1)n∂n∂yn and Hn(−x)=(−1)nHn(x) is immediate. ◻

One may also prove using properties of F in definition 1.1.2, as ∂F∂x=tF,∂F∂t=(x−t)F and F(−x,t)=F(x,−t) .

The following lemma shows that Hermite polynomial acting on two standard centered Gaussian variable yields orthogonal-like result.

Lemma 1.1.4. (Orthogonality of centered Gaussian variables acted by Hermite polynomials) Let X,Y be two random variable with joint Gaussian distribution s.t. E(X)=E(Y)=0 and E(X2)=E(Y2)=1 . Then for all n,m⩾0 , we have

E(Hn(X)Hm(Y))=δmn1n![E(XY)]n

Proof. Note that F(x,t)=exp⁡(tx−t22) could be rewritten to series related to Hn(x) , we consider taking expectation of F(X,t) and F(Y,t) . On the one hand, we have

E[F(X,s)F(Y,t)]=E[exp⁡(sX−s22)exp⁡(tY−t22)]=exp⁡(−s2+t22)E[exp⁡(sX+tY)]Z=sX+tY is centered Gaussian=exp⁡(−s2+t22)∫−∞+∞12πσexp⁡(z−z22σ)dz=exp⁡(−s2+t22+σ2)∫−∞+∞12πσexp⁡(−(z−σ)22σ)dz=exp⁡(−s2+t22)exp⁡(stE[XY])σ=E[Z2]=2stE[XY]=exp⁡(−s2+t22)∑k=0∞(stE[XY])nn!

On the other hand, we have

E[F(X,s)F(Y,t)]=E{[∑n=0∞sn⋅Hn(X)][∑m=0∞tm⋅Hm(Y)]}=E[∑m,n=0∞smtnHn(X)Hm(Y)]=∑m,n=0∞smtnE[Hn(X)Hm(Y)]

Comparing the order of smtn results in what we need to prove. ◻

In the following we will show that random variables of the form Hn(W(h)) spans the space L2(Ω,F,P) . Let Hn be the closed linear subspace generated by the random variables {Hn(W(h)):h∈H,‖h‖H=1} . We force the norm of h to 1 , since by the linearity of W(⋅) any W(h),h∈H is equal to cW(h′) in which c is a constant and h′ has norm 1 . As W(h) is a centered Gaussian variable, using lemma 1.1.4, we have Hn⊥Hm if n≠m . To show L2(Ω,F,P)=⨁n=1∞Hn , we only need to prove that "if X is perpendicular to all subspaces Hn , X shall only be zero", otherwise X must be a linear combination of the vectors in Hn s. Formally, "pick X∈L2(Ω,F,P) such that for all n⩾0 and all uniform vector h∈H , we have E[XHn(W(h))]=0 , this would result in X=0 ". This is equivalent to " E[X(W(h))n]=0 implies x=0 ". Further more, we shall prove " E[Xexp⁡(W(h))]=0 implies X=0 ", and this gives up to the following lemma.

Lemma 1.1.5. Random variables {exp⁡(W(h)):h∈H} form a total(dense) subset of L2(Ω,G,P) , in which G is the σ -algebra generated by {W(h):h∈H} .

Proof. To prove {exp⁡(W(h)):h∈H} forms a dense subset of the Hilbert space L2(Ω,G,P) , we only need to prove the set of vectors spans the total space. This is equivalent to the statement:

⟨X,exp⁡(W(h))⟩=0 for all h∈H⟺X=0.

Therefore pick X∈L2(Ω,G,P) such that for all h∈H , E[Xexp⁡(W(h))]=0 . Fix m and pick h1,…,hm∈H and let h∈∑i=1mtihi , the linearity tells E[Xexp⁡(∑i=1mtiW(hi))]=0 . To prove X=0 , it suffices to prove ∫GXdP=E[X1G]=0 for all G∈G , which is equivalent to showing E[X1B(W(h1),…,W(hm))]=0 in which B∈B(Rm) , as G are generated by cylinder sets {ω∈Ω:(W(h1)(ω),…,W(hm)(ω))∈B,B∈B(Rm)} . Note that E[X1B(W(h1),…,W(hm))] could be interpreted as a signed measure on (Rm,B(Rm)) :

ν(B)=E[X1B(W(h1),…,W(hm))]

note that ∫1Bdν=ν(B)=E[X1B(W(h1),…,W(hm))] one could prove that ∫fdν=E[Xf(W(h1),…,W(hm))] by linearity and monotonic convergence theorem. Therefore we consider the Laplace transform to get an exponential in our integral and exactly meets the result we just arrived at:

ν~(t)=∫Rme⟨t,y⟩dν(y)=E[Xexp⁡(∑i=1mtiW(hi))]=0.

As B∈B is randomly chosen, by the injectivity of Laplace transform, we have ν(B)=E[X1B(W(h1),…,W(hm))]≡0 and this results holds for all m and all h1,…,hm∈H . Therefore E[X1A]≡0 for all cylinder set A . Finally by the monotone class theorem, we have E[X,1G]=0 for all G∈G . ◻

With lemma 1.1.5, we are able to prove the Wiener chaos expansion theorem.

Wiener chaos expansion

Theorem 1.1.6. (Wiener chaos expansion) The space L2(Ω,G,P) can be decomposed to infinite orthogonal sums of Hn :

L2(Ω,G,P)=⨁n=0∞Hn

Proof. Consider a similar approach in lemma 1.1.5. Pick X∈L2(Ω,F,P) such that X is orthogonal to all Hn , i.e. E[XHn(W(h))]=0 for all n≥0 and h∈H,‖h‖H=1 . As xn can be written by a linear combination of Hm in which m≤n , thus we have E[X(W(h))n]=0 for all n and h , and therefore E[Xexp⁡[tW(h)]]=0 for all t∈R . Acording to lemma 1.1.5, we deduce X=0 . ◻

Next we consider constructing a orthogonal system of spaces Hn and admit the case when H is infinite dimensional. We want to utilize the orthogonal properties of Hermite polynomials, such that every F∈Hn could be written in a linear combination (or series) of something related to Hermite polynomial.

We start with polynomials of degrees up to n . Let Pn0 be the space spanned by random variables p(W(h1),…,W(hk)) , where k⩾1 , h1,…,hk∈H and p is a real polynomials in k variables such that deg(p)⩽n . Note that Pn0 is not a closed set in L2(Ω,F,P) , take Sn=∑i=1n2−iW2(ei) , in which ei are orthogonal base vectors in H . This means W(ei) s are independent standard Gaussian random variables, as the definition of isonormal Gaussian process puts: E[W(ei)W(ej)]=⟨ei,ej⟩H=δij . Sn has a limit in L2 , take m<n , we have

E[(Sn−Sm)2]=E[(∑i=mn2−iW2(ei))2]=∑i=mn2−2iE[W4(ei)]+∑j<k21−j−kE[W2(ej)W2(ek)]⩽2−2(m−1)E[W4(ei)]+2−2mE[W2(ej)W2(ek)]

we conclude that Sn is a Cauchy sequence in L2 and therefore has a limit S . We then prove S is not in Pn0 . Assume S=p(W(h1),…,W(hk)) for some k and h1,…,hk∈H , then one could always find a sufficiently large j such that ej⊥{h1,…,hk} , which leads to contradiction.

We use the term "orthogonal system" instead of "basis" sometimes. The latter one says each h∈H can be written by linear combinations of finite base vectors.

In summary, taking a closure of Pn0 is crutial, we denote the closure Pn0― of Pn0 in L2 be Pn , and we claim that it is the orthogonal sum of H0 through Hn .

Lemma 1.1.7. The closure of Pn0 in L2 can be decomposed to orthogonal sum of Wiener chaos subspaces H0 through Hn :

Pn=⨁i=0nHi

Proof. On the one hand, we begin with Hi(W(h)) , which is apprently a polynomial and belongs to Pn0 . Furthermore, we have the finite linear combination of Hi(W(hi)) is still in Pn0 , i.e. Hi0=span{Hi(W(h)):h∈H}⊂Pn0 . When taking the closure of both Hi0 and Pn0 , one can see that all clusterpoints in Hi are also cluster points in Pn , thus Hi⊂Pn . Finally, since i is arbitrary, Hi,i=0,…,n are subsets of Pn , which gives their finite orthogonal sum is also contained by Pn . On the other hand, To show Pn⊂⨁i=0nHi , it is enough to show that Pn is orthogonal to all Hm such that m>n , in other words, we need to show E[p(W(h1),…,W(hk))Hm(W(h0))]=0 for all h0,…,hk,‖h‖=1 , m>n and polynomial p with degree less than or equals n . By the linearity of W(⋅) we can always rewrite p(W(h1),…,W(hk)) using q(W(e1),…,W(ej),W(h)) , where {e1,…,ej,h} is a orthognormal family for some polynomial q whose degree is also less than or equals n . Expanding Ep(W(e1),…,W(ej),W(h))Hm(W(h)) would yield a linear combinations of mononomials like Wα1(e1)⋯Wαj(ej)Wαh(h)Hm(W(h)) , which could be decomposed since W(h) and other W(ei) s are independent:

E[Wα1(e1)⋯Wαj(ej)Wr(h)Hm(W(h))]=E[∏i=1jWαi(ei)]E[Wr(h)Hm(W(h))],

in which α1+⋯+αj+r⩽n . To show E[p(W(h1),…,W(hk))Hm(W(h0))]=0 , it is enough to show for all r⩽n<m , we have E[Wr(h)Hm(h)]=0 , which is immediate since Wr(h) could be expressed as linear combinations of Hermite polynomials with degrees less than r . ◻

Taking closure of Pn0 and Hi0 s let Pn and Hi contains series made by similar mononomials, however to ensure we find orthonormal system in Hn we seek to link this series of mononomials with Hermite polynomials. With this idea in mind, we need to construct random variables like Ha1(W(e1))Ha2(W(e2))⋯Han(W(en)) to construct aforementioned polynomials (as p(W(h1),…,W(hk)) could always be expressed as p(∑i1=1∞a1iW(ei),…,∑ik=1∞akiW(ei)) in which ∑i1=1∞ani<∞,n=1,…,k ).

Finding Orthonormal Basis of Hn

Definition 1.1.8. (Generalized Hermite polynomials) We denote Λ be the set of all series a=(a1,a2,…),ai∈N whose indices are zero except finite number of them. Given multiindex a∈Λ , define a!:=∏i=1∞ai and |a|:=∑i=1∞ai . Generalized Hermite polynomial with multiindex a is defined as

Ha(x)=∏i=1∞Hai(xi)

Let {ei:i⩾1} be the orthonormal basis of infinite-dimensional Hilbert space H , we define a random variable using similar manner:

Φa:=a!∏i=1∞Hai(W(ei)),

which are the building blocks we are looking for. Moreover, Φa exhibits similar orthogonal properties as ordinary Hermite polynomials. Indeed, for any a,b∈Λ , we have

E[ΦaΦb]=E[a!b!∏i=1∞Hai(W(ei))Hbi(W(ei))]=a!b!∏i=1∞E[Hai(W(ei))Hbi(W(ei))]={1,a=b;0,a≠b.◻

To this point, we could probe that {Φa:|a|=n} is a complete orthonormal syetem in Hn :

Proposition 1.1.9. (Orthonormal system of Hn ) For any n⩾1 , the random variables {Φa:|a|=n} form a complete orthonormal system in Hn .

Proof. One could immediately see that {Φa:|a|=n} is a orthonormal system as E[ΦaΦb]=δab . On the other hand, consider a union of such sets of random variables instead:

⋃i=0n{Φa:|a|=i}.

Polynomials p(W(h1),…,W(hk)) in Pn could be approximated by W(e1),…,W(ej) , whose polynomials could then be expressed by random variables in {Φa,|a|⩽n} . However if we substitute n to n−1 , we have {Φa:|a|⩽n−1} forms a complete orthonormal system of Pn−1 therefore {Φa:|a|=n} forms a complete orthogonal system of Hn , as Pn=H0⊕⋯⊕Hn . Furthermore, {Φa:a∈Λ} is a complete orthonormal system of L2(Ω,F,P) . ◻

Ito Isometry of High Oder Chaos

In the end of this small section, we consider similar isometry as the Ito isometry that works in H1 . In the definition of isometric Gaussian process, we have the isometry of oder 1 as W:h↦W(h) , i.e. ei↦W(ei) by the linearity of W and assume H is infinite-dimensional. As we constructed Φa above, we seek some object that is mapped to Φa or some multiple of Φa , which also satisfy the requirements to be an isometry like oder one case: ⟨W(h),W(g)⟩L2=⟨h,g⟩H , or ‖W(h)‖L22=‖h‖H2 . Associated with each Φa , there is a list (ek1,…,ek1,ek2,…,ek2,…,ekm,…,ekm) , in which ei shows up ai times (and those ei with ai=0 don't show up in this list), and the length of this list is n . Moreover, as the number of copies of each base vector ei is known, we don't care about their order. The symmetric tensor product in mathematics is such an space whose vectors don't care about order. Consider e1⊗⋯⊗ek∈H⊗k , define the symmetric map be

symm(e1⊗⋯⊗ek):=1k!∑σ∈Sneσ(1)⊗⋯⊗eσ(k)

in which σ is a permutation. In this end, we can construct the linear map In . Take a∈Λ such that |a|=n , and give the outcome of In acting on all base vectors in symmetric tensor product space H⊗^n :

In[symm(⊗i=1∞ei⊗ai)]↦Φa.

Then we consider an appropriate norm on H⊗^n . A typical choice is the norm ∥⋅∥H⊗n :

∥a1⊗⋯⊗an∥H⊗n2=∏i=1n‖ai‖H2

Thus we have

∥symm(⊗i=1∞ei⊗ai)∥H⊗n2=‖1n!∑σ∈Snσ(⊗i=1∞ei⊗ai)‖H⊗n2=‖a!n!∑i=1n!/a!wi‖H⊗n2De-duplicated orthonormalvectors in H⊗^n=(a!n!)2∑i=1n!/a!‖wi‖H⊗n2=a!n!.

To construct an isometry, it is enough to let the norm of H⊗^n be n!∥⋅∥H⊗n while modifying the linear map In to be

In[symm(⊗i=1∞ei⊗ai)]↦a!Φa.

This gives an isometry between H⊗^n and Hn . Moreover, we can put H⊗^n all toghether and form so-called Fock space ⊕n=0∞n!H⊗^n and thus it is isometric to L2(Ω,F,P) .
